sources.title: Brian 2, an intuitive and efficient neural simulator
sources.authors: M. Stimberg, R. Brette, D. F. M. Goodman
locators: eLife article body, sections read: Abstract, eLife digest, Introduction, Materials and methods (Design and implementation; Mathematical level; Computational experiment level; Implementation level), Discussion, Appendix 1 (Design details)
"Differential equations are specified in strings using mathematical notation" (Materials and methods)
"Standalone mode executes an independent binary file compiled from C++ code" (Materials and methods)
"Brian2GeNN uses the GPU-enhanced Neural Network simulator (GeNN) to accelerate simulations" (Discussion)
sources.notes: Canonical reference paper for Brian2, body read directly from eLife (open access). Confirms bibliographic metadata (Stimberg, Brette, Goodman; eLife 2019; doi 10.7554/eLife.47314). Executes: neuron/synapse dynamics specified as differential equations in strings, supporting hybrid continuous+discrete-event systems, point integrate-and-fire neurons, graded synapses, and limited multi-compartment models. Runs on: CPU by default (Python runtime mode calling C++ via the weave library, or a standalone mode compiling to an independent C++ binary) across Windows, OS X, and Linux; GPU acceleration is reached only through separate companion projects Brian2GeNN (via the GeNN simulator) and the then-ongoing Brian2CUDA, not Brian2 itself. Reaches: no neuromorphic hardware backend stated anywhere in the body read. A run can claim: numerical simulation of the specified differential-equation model, not hardware execution.

sources.title: NEST simulator documentation
locators: https://nest-simulator.readthedocs.io/en/stable/ ("Welcome to the NEST Simulator documentation!")
https://nest-simulator.readthedocs.io/en/stable/models/index.html ("Model directory")
https://nest-simulator.readthedocs.io/en/stable/installation/index.html ("Install and run NEST")
sources.notes: NEST's own documentation, created because the only prior registry hit for NEST (vanalbada2018-spinnaker-nest) is a SpiNNaker-vs-NEST comparison paper, not NEST's own page. Executes: "NEST is used in computational neuroscience to model and study behavior of large networks of neurons"; the model directory states NEST "has over 100 models" of neurons, synapses, and devices, including leaky/exponential/adaptive integrate-and-fire variants, Hodgkin-Huxley, Izhikevich, static and short-term-plasticity (Tsodyks) synapses, STDP variants, and gap junctions. Runs on: installable on Linux, macOS, Windows, and cross-platform Docker, with a dedicated guide to "Optimize performance of HPC Systems" and a "Guide to parallel computing"; no GPU support stated on the pages read. Reaches: no neuromorphic hardware backend stated on the pages read. A run can claim: "A NEST simulation is created with input from stimulation devices, neuron models, and synapse models, along with connection rules", i.e. a numerical simulation of network dynamics, not hardware execution.

sources.title: The NEURON simulator documentation
locators: https://www.neuronsimulator.org/en/latest/ (landing page, redirect target of https://nrn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)
sources.notes: NEURON's own documentation, created because the only prior registry hit for NEURON (SJ-NeuronDocs) is a SpikingJelly tutorial page, not NEURON's own page. Only the landing page was read; quickstart.html and about.html both returned 404 on this pass. Executes: "NEURON is a simulator for neurons and networks of neurons"; the page does not state which neuron/model classes (compartmental, ion-channel-based, or otherwise) it executes. Runs on: "runs efficiently on your local machine, in the cloud, or on an HPC", with mentions of Google Colab, the Neuroscience Gateway, and EBRAINS as hosted options; no CPU/GPU/MPI parallelization detail stated. Reaches: no neuromorphic hardware backend stated on the page read. A run can claim: the page only says users "Build and simulate models using Python, HOC, and/or NEURON's graphical interface"; it does not characterize what kind of dynamics a run represents.

sources.title: GeNN (GPU-enhanced Neuronal Networks)
locators: https://genn-team.github.io/ (GeNN project homepage)
https://genn-team.github.io/genn/documentation/4/html/d2/dba/SpineML.html ("GeNN: SpineML and SpineCreator", GeNN 4.9.0 documentation body page, fix round 2)
sources.notes: GeNN's own project homepage, created because the only prior registry hit for GeNN (Turner22-mlGeNN) is the mlGeNN paper, a variant library built on GeNN, not GeNN's own page. Executes: "GeNN is a GPU enhanced Neuronal Network simulation environment based on NVIDIA CUDA technology", described as "a code generation framework for accelerated brain simulations" (code-generated neuron/synapse model simulations, model classes not enumerated on this page). Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA; the page states no CPU-only execution path. Reaches: no neuromorphic hardware backend stated; the homepage instead cites a claim that GPUs running GeNN "Outperform Current HPC and Neuromorphic Solutions in Terms of Speed and Energy When Simulating a Highly-Connected Cortical Model" (i.e. GeNN is offered as an alternative to neuromorphic hardware, not a path onto it). A run can claim: GPU-executed code-generated simulation of the specified brain model. Maintained by the GeNN Team (J. Knight, T. Nowotny, University of Sussex); foundational publication Yavuz et al. 2016, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/srep18854, cited by the team page but its body not itself re-read for this record. Fix round 2 added a documentation body page (not the homepage): the SpineML integration page, GeNN 4.9.0. It walks through configuring SpineCreator to use a GeNN installation as a simulator and running an experiment, and it names a "GENN_SPINEML_CPU_ONLY" environment variable for CPU-only operation of the SpineML integration, which qualifies the homepage's "no CPU-only execution path" statement, that path exists at least for this integration. retrieval_status stays full_text, now supported by a documentation body page, not only the landing page.

sources.title: Samna documentation
locators: https://synsense-sys-int.gitlab.io/samna/0.48.6/index.html ("Welcome to Samna's Documentation!", redirect target of https://synsense-sys-int.gitlab.io/samna/)
https://synsense-sys-int.gitlab.io/samna/0.46.1/models/speckSeries/summary.html ("Speck Series", a chip-specific samna documentation page, fix round 2)
sources.notes: SynSense's own samna documentation. Created because samna was previously covered only by a Rockpool Xylo record and a Sinabs Speck-deployment tutorial, both different tools. States "Samna is the API to interact with SynSense devices from your PC", providing device configuration, event-data routing, and device management via Python bindings run on a host PC. The landing page's table of contents references "Chip Models" and "Development Kits" sections but this page itself does not enumerate Speck, Xylo, or DYNAP by name; deeper chip-specific pages were not fetched in this pass. A run can claim: direct interaction with and control of the physical SynSense device from the host, not a simulation. Fix round 2 added a chip-specific documentation body page under the samna docs site (Speck Series, v0.46.1). It names and describes the chip directly, "Speck is a comprehensive, multicore spiking neural network processing chip which is able to support large-scale spiking convolutional neural network (SCNN) with an fully asynchronous chip architecture", integrating a DVS sensor for event-driven visual sensing at few-ms response latency and milliwatt-scale power. This resolves the earlier note that the landing page alone did not name Speck. retrieval_status stays full_text, now supported by a chip-specific documentation page, not only the landing page.

No neuromorphic hardware backends; simulation-only. Supports Linux and macOS with CMake build system. 2026-09-17, fix round 1 of the whole-branch review: the record is documentation, the CARLsim 5 repository README; the earlier title (the README's tagline), author list (the CARLsim 4 citation the README gives) and year (2013) were not stated on the page as the README's own bibliographic fields and are now null or replaced.

Read via the arXiv mirror (ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2004.06061); the published IEEE Xplore version carries the doi above. The paper reimplements IBM TrueNorth's five per-core components (neuron block, core SRAM, router, scheduler, token controller) as a reference design realized on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC ZCU102 development board (XCZU9EG FPGA), then validates it against IBM's own Compass simulator on MNIST and vector-matrix-multiplication case studies.
